audit-sampling-methodology#summary.title: Audit Sampling Methodology
audit-sampling-methodology#summary.text: A two-stage sampling approach used across substantive and controls testing: Stage 1 stratifies the population by risk (dollar value, complexity, prior-year exceptions) so higher-risk items get more attention; Stage 2 applies statistical or judgmental sample selection within each stratum to pick the actual items tested.

audit-sampling-methodology#section-why-s.title: Audit Sampling Methodology
audit-sampling-methodology#section-why-s.heading: Why Sample at All
audit-sampling-methodology#section-why-s.text:
## Why Sample at All

Testing every transaction in a population is rarely feasible or
necessary — sampling lets the audit draw a conclusion about the whole
population from testing a subset, provided the sample is selected and
sized in a way that supports that inference. The two questions every
sampling plan has to answer are: which items get selected, and how many.

audit-sampling-methodology#section-stage.title: Audit Sampling Methodology
audit-sampling-methodology#section-stage.heading: Stage 1: Risk Stratification
audit-sampling-methodology#section-stage.text:
## Stage 1: Risk Stratification

Before selecting any items, split the population into strata by risk
characteristics — dollar value (e.g. above/below a materiality-linked
threshold), transaction complexity (manual journal entries vs. system-
generated), and known risk factors (prior-year exceptions, related-party
transactions, override of automated controls). High-risk strata get
tested more thoroughly than low-risk strata; this is what lets the audit
concentrate effort where a misstatement is more likely, rather than
spreading equal attention across a population where most of the risk sits
in a small fraction of the items.

audit-sampling-methodology#section-stage.title: Audit Sampling Methodology
audit-sampling-methodology#section-stage.heading: Stage 2: Sample Selection Within Strata
audit-sampling-methodology#section-stage.text:
## Stage 2: Sample Selection Within Strata

Within each stratum, select the actual sample using either statistical
methods (random sampling with a calculated sample size based on
confidence level, tolerable error, and expected error rate) or judgmental
selection (targeting specific high-risk items directly — large dollar
items, unusual account combinations, items flagged by data analytics).
Statistical sampling supports a quantified conclusion about the whole
stratum; judgmental sampling is faster and often used for the highest-risk
items where 100% coverage of the largest few transactions is more
efficient than a statistical draw.

audit-sampling-methodology#section-evalu.title: Audit Sampling Methodology
audit-sampling-methodology#section-evalu.heading: Evaluating Results
audit-sampling-methodology#section-evalu.text:
## Evaluating Results

If a sample turns up exceptions, project the error rate back to the
stratum's population value (for statistical samples) and assess whether
the projected misstatement, combined with other findings, could exceed
performance materiality. A single exception in a small statistical sample
can imply a large potential population error — don't dismiss it without
running the projection.

contract-compliance-testing#summary.title: Contract Compliance Testing
contract-compliance-testing#summary.text: Tests whether billed amounts, rebates, and service levels under a significant vendor or customer contract actually match the negotiated contract terms, since contract terms are frequently administered manually outside the system that generates the invoice.

contract-compliance-testing#section-why-.title: Contract Compliance Testing
contract-compliance-testing#section-why-.heading: Why Contract Terms Drift From Practice
contract-compliance-testing#section-why-.text:
## Why Contract Terms Drift From Practice

Negotiated contract terms — volume discounts, rebate thresholds, service-
level commitments, most-favored-customer clauses — are often tracked in
the contract document itself rather than configured into the billing or
procurement system, which creates a real risk that invoicing and payment
simply follow whatever the system defaults to rather than what was
actually negotiated. Testing exists specifically to catch that drift.

contract-compliance-testing#section-pric.title: Contract Compliance Testing
contract-compliance-testing#section-pric.heading: Pricing and Rebate Verification
contract-compliance-testing#section-pric.text:
## Pricing and Rebate Verification

Select a sample of invoices or payments under the in-scope contract and
independently recalculate the amount that should have been billed or paid
per the contract's actual pricing schedule, rebate tiers, and any
volume-based thresholds — comparing against the negotiated document, not
against a system-generated price list that may not reflect the real
agreement. Where a rebate is owed based on cumulative volume, confirm the
volume calculation used the correct measurement period and that the
rebate was actually paid or credited, not just calculated and left
outstanding.

contract-compliance-testing#section-serv.title: Contract Compliance Testing
contract-compliance-testing#section-serv.heading: Service Level Compliance
contract-compliance-testing#section-serv.text:
## Service Level Compliance

For contracts with defined service-level commitments (response time,
uptime, delivery windows), obtain the vendor's or the internal team's
performance data for the period and independently verify whether
commitments were actually met, and — where they weren't — whether the
contractually specified penalty or credit was actually applied. A
service-level breach that goes unenforced represents value the
organization is entitled to but isn't collecting.

contract-compliance-testing#section-cont.title: Contract Compliance Testing
contract-compliance-testing#section-cont.heading: Contract Renewal and Auto-Renewal Risk
contract-compliance-testing#section-cont.text:
## Contract Renewal and Auto-Renewal Risk

Review contracts approaching their renewal or auto-renewal date and
confirm the business has actually re-evaluated pricing and terms rather
than letting the contract auto-renew on stale terms — a contract that
auto-renewed multiple times without renegotiation is a common way an
organization ends up paying above-market rates without anyone
specifically deciding that outcome.

data-analytics-in-internal-audit#summary.title: Data Analytics in Internal Audit
data-analytics-in-internal-audit#summary.text: Overview of how data analytics is used across internal audit procedures — full-population testing instead of small samples, targeted exception flagging, and continuous monitoring between audits — and where each technique shows up elsewhere in this corpus.

data-analytics-in-internal-audit#section.title: Data Analytics in Internal Audit
data-analytics-in-internal-audit#section.heading: Full-Population Testing
data-analytics-in-internal-audit#section.text:
## Full-Population Testing

Where transaction data is available electronically, analytics lets an
audit test 100% of a population instead of a small sample — every journal
entry, every vendor payment, every access grant — which catches issues a
sample could statistically miss entirely. [Journal Entry
Testing](journal-entry-testing.md) and [Segregation of Duties
Review](segregation-of-duties-review.md) both rely on full-population
analytics rather than sampling for exactly this reason: the population of
interest (entries matching risk criteria, users holding conflicting
access) is small relative to the whole population, and a sample could
easily land zero hits even when real issues exist.

data-analytics-in-internal-audit#section.title: Data Analytics in Internal Audit
data-analytics-in-internal-audit#section.heading: Exception Flagging and Pattern Detection
data-analytics-in-internal-audit#section.text:
## Exception Flagging and Pattern Detection

Analytics is also used to flag specific patterns worth a closer look
rather than test everything equally — duplicate vendor detection in
[Vendor Master Data Control Testing](vendor-master-data-control-testing.md),
split-transaction detection in [Expense Reimbursement
Testing](expense-reimbursement-testing.md), and fuzzy matching against
employee records for fraud indicators. The common thread is defining a
specific, testable pattern in advance rather than browsing data hoping
something looks wrong.

data-analytics-in-internal-audit#section.title: Data Analytics in Internal Audit
data-analytics-in-internal-audit#section.heading: Continuous Monitoring Between Audits
data-analytics-in-internal-audit#section.text:
## Continuous Monitoring Between Audits

Beyond a single audit engagement, analytics can run on a recurring
schedule to flag risk indicators between formal audits — a dashboard
re-running the SoD conflict matrix monthly, or a report re-scoring journal
entries against risk criteria every close cycle — so issues surface closer
to when they occur rather than waiting for the next scheduled audit to
catch them.

expense-reimbursement-testing#summary.title: Expense Reimbursement Testing
expense-reimbursement-testing#summary.text: Tests employee expense reports for policy compliance, proper approval, and receipt support, with particular attention to split transactions used to stay under approval or receipt thresholds.

expense-reimbursement-testing#section-ob.title: Expense Reimbursement Testing
expense-reimbursement-testing#section-ob.heading: Objective
expense-reimbursement-testing#section-ob.text:
## Objective

Confirm employee expense reimbursements comply with the travel and
expense (T&E) policy, are supported by adequate documentation, and were
approved by someone with actual authority over the employee's spending —
not just routed through an approval workflow that rubber-stamps whatever
is submitted.

expense-reimbursement-testing#section-do.title: Expense Reimbursement Testing
expense-reimbursement-testing#section-do.heading: Documentation and Policy Compliance
expense-reimbursement-testing#section-do.text:
## Documentation and Policy Compliance

For each sampled expense report, confirm an itemized receipt exists for
every line item above the policy's no-receipt threshold, the expense
category matches the policy's allowable list, and any exception to policy
(e.g. a meal over the per-person limit) has an explicit business
justification attached, not just the manager's approval alone. A manager
approval without a justification note for an over-policy item should be
treated as a documentation exception even if the approval itself is
genuine.

expense-reimbursement-testing#section-ap.title: Expense Reimbursement Testing
expense-reimbursement-testing#section-ap.heading: Approval Authority Testing
expense-reimbursement-testing#section-ap.text:
## Approval Authority Testing

Confirm the approver on each sampled report is actually the employee's
manager or someone with delegated approval authority for that employee —
self-approval, or approval by a peer rather than a manager, is a
segregation-of-duties failure regardless of whether the expense itself
was legitimate. Cross-reference the approver against the HR org chart
current as of the expense date, not the current org chart, since
reporting lines change.

expense-reimbursement-testing#section-sp.title: Expense Reimbursement Testing
expense-reimbursement-testing#section-sp.heading: Split-Transaction Detection
expense-reimbursement-testing#section-sp.text:
## Split-Transaction Detection

Run expense data analytics to flag employees with multiple same-day,
same-vendor transactions that individually fall under a receipt or
approval threshold but sum above it — a common pattern for deliberately
avoiding scrutiny. A single instance may be coincidental (two separate
business meals); a pattern across multiple months for the same employee
warrants follow-up regardless of whether any individual transaction looks
suspicious on its own.

it-user-access-review#summary.title: IT User Access Review
it-user-access-review#summary.text: Periodic review of who has access to financially significant systems, testing new-access provisioning, timely termination/transfer deprovisioning, and privileged/admin access against least-privilege and segregation-of-duties expectations.

it-user-access-review#section-scope.title: IT User Access Review
it-user-access-review#section-scope.heading: Scope
it-user-access-review#section-scope.text:
## Scope

Covers user access to systems that support financial reporting or
process financial transactions — the ERP, treasury/banking platforms,
and any system feeding a SOX-relevant control. Access reviews for systems
outside this scope may still matter for security purposes but aren't part
of the ICFR-relevant review.

it-user-access-review#section-new-access.title: IT User Access Review
it-user-access-review#section-new-access.heading: New Access Provisioning
it-user-access-review#section-new-access.text:
## New Access Provisioning

Sample new user access grants during the period and confirm each was
requested through the formal access-request process, approved by the
requesting employee's manager and (for financially sensitive roles) by
the relevant system/data owner, and that the access granted matches what
was actually approved — not a broader role assigned for convenience.
Access that exceeds what was approved is a finding even if it was never
misused; the control being tested is the provisioning process, not
whether harm resulted.

it-user-access-review#section-terminatio.title: IT User Access Review
it-user-access-review#section-terminatio.heading: Termination and Transfer Deprovisioning
it-user-access-review#section-terminatio.text:
## Termination and Transfer Deprovisioning

Compare the HR termination/transfer report for the period against system
access logs to confirm access was removed or adjusted within the policy's
required window (commonly 24-48 hours for terminations). A terminated
employee who retains system access even briefly is a significant finding,
since it's exactly the population most likely to have both motive and a
narrowing window of opportunity. Internal transfers need equal attention:
access from the old role should be removed, not just supplemented with
access for the new one, or the employee accumulates access across roles
over time.

it-user-access-review#section-privileged.title: IT User Access Review
it-user-access-review#section-privileged.heading: Privileged Access and Segregation of Duties
it-user-access-review#section-privileged.text:
## Privileged Access and Segregation of Duties

Review the list of users with administrative or privileged access
(ability to bypass application controls, directly modify data, or grant
access to others) and confirm the population is limited to roles that
genuinely require it, each has a documented business justification, and
no privileged user also holds an incompatible transactional role — e.g.
someone who can both create vendors and approve payments. Privileged
access should also be logged and periodically reviewed by someone other
than the privileged user.

journal-entry-testing#summary.title: Journal Entry Testing
journal-entry-testing#summary.text: Data-analytics-driven review of manual journal entries, using risk criteria (timing, size, account combinations, poster/approver patterns) to select a targeted subset rather than a random sample, since manual entries are the most common vehicle for management override of controls.

journal-entry-testing#section-why-journa.title: Journal Entry Testing
journal-entry-testing#section-why-journa.heading: Why Journal Entries Get Targeted Testing
journal-entry-testing#section-why-journa.text:
## Why Journal Entries Get Targeted Testing

Manual journal entries bypass the automated controls built into
transaction-processing systems, which makes them the classic vehicle for
management override of controls — the risk that professional standards
specifically call out as present in every audit regardless of how strong
the rest of the control environment looks. Because of this, journal entry
testing is risk-targeted rather than randomly sampled.

journal-entry-testing#section-risk-crite.title: Journal Entry Testing
journal-entry-testing#section-risk-crite.heading: Risk Criteria for Selection
journal-entry-testing#section-risk-crite.text:
## Risk Criteria for Selection

Pull the full population of manual journal entries for the period and
flag entries matching risk criteria: postings made late at night or on
weekends, entries posted and approved by the same user, round-dollar
entries, entries to accounts with a history of manipulation (reserves,
accruals, unusual account pairings), and entries made in the days
immediately before period-end close. An entry matching several criteria
at once is higher risk than one matching a single criterion, so score
entries rather than treating every flag as equally significant.

journal-entry-testing#section-testing-se.title: Journal Entry Testing
journal-entry-testing#section-testing-se.heading: Testing Selected Entries
journal-entry-testing#section-testing-se.text:
## Testing Selected Entries

For each selected entry, obtain supporting documentation for the business
rationale, confirm the account coding is appropriate for the transaction
described, and verify the approval — if the system allows a preparer to
also approve their own entry, that itself is a control gap worth noting
independent of whether any individual entry looks improper. An entry with
no supporting documentation beyond "correcting entry" is a finding
regardless of whether the correction turns out to be legitimate.

journal-entry-testing#section-aggregatin.title: Journal Entry Testing
journal-entry-testing#section-aggregatin.heading: Aggregating Findings
journal-entry-testing#section-aggregatin.text:
## Aggregating Findings

Individual journal entry exceptions should be aggregated and evaluated
together, not just closed one at a time — a pattern of similar entries
from the same preparer, or a cluster of adjustments to the same account
across multiple periods, can indicate a systemic issue that no single
entry would reveal on its own.

physical-inventory-observation#summary.title: Physical Inventory Observation
physical-inventory-observation#summary.text: On-site observation of a physical inventory count, testing both the client's count procedures and independently test-counting a sample to compare against the perpetual inventory system.

physical-inventory-observation#section-o.title: Physical Inventory Observation
physical-inventory-observation#section-o.heading: Objective
physical-inventory-observation#section-o.text:
## Objective

Obtain firsthand evidence that inventory recorded in the perpetual system
actually exists, in the condition and quantity recorded, by observing the
client's physical count and independently test-counting a sample rather
than relying solely on the client's count sheets.

physical-inventory-observation#section-p.title: Physical Inventory Observation
physical-inventory-observation#section-p.heading: Pre-Count Planning
physical-inventory-observation#section-p.text:
## Pre-Count Planning

Before the count date, confirm the count instructions issued to count
teams cover cutoff procedures (how receiving and shipping are handled
during the count), how count teams are assigned to avoid a team counting
an area they normally manage, and how obsolete, damaged, or slow-moving
inventory is identified and tagged separately during the count rather than
counted at full value alongside good inventory.

physical-inventory-observation#section-o.title: Physical Inventory Observation
physical-inventory-observation#section-o.heading: Observing the Count
physical-inventory-observation#section-o.text:
## Observing the Count

During the count, observe whether count teams are actually following the
issued instructions — proper two-person count-and-recount teams, tags
sequentially controlled so none are lost or duplicated, and no
uncontrolled movement of inventory in or out of the counted area while
counting is in progress. Independently test-count a risk-based sample of
items (high-dollar items, items with prior-period discrepancies, and a
selection from each major location) and compare test counts against both
the client's count sheets and the perpetual system quantity on hand.

physical-inventory-observation#section-c.title: Physical Inventory Observation
physical-inventory-observation#section-c.heading: Cutoff and Reconciliation
physical-inventory-observation#section-c.text:
## Cutoff and Reconciliation

Record the last shipping and receiving document numbers used before the
count and the first ones used after, so cutoff can be tested later against
the recorded sale or purchase — inventory in transit at the count date is
a common source of double-counting or omission if cutoff isn't pinned down
precisely. After the count, obtain the client's reconciliation of count
results to the perpetual system and evaluate whether the resulting
adjustment is consistent with the discrepancies actually observed during
the count, not just accepted as given.

revenue-recognition-testing#summary.title: Revenue Recognition Testing
revenue-recognition-testing#summary.text: Tests whether recognized revenue reflects performance obligations actually satisfied in the period, with emphasis on cutoff around period-end and multi-element arrangements where allocation judgment drives the recognized amount.

revenue-recognition-testing#section-obje.title: Revenue Recognition Testing
revenue-recognition-testing#section-obje.heading: Objective
revenue-recognition-testing#section-obje.text:
## Objective

Confirm revenue recognized in the period reflects performance obligations
that were actually satisfied — goods delivered, services rendered, or
milestones met per the contract terms — rather than revenue pulled
forward or pushed back to hit a period's targets.

revenue-recognition-testing#section-cuto.title: Revenue Recognition Testing
revenue-recognition-testing#section-cuto.heading: Cutoff Testing
revenue-recognition-testing#section-cuto.text:
## Cutoff Testing

Sample transactions recorded in the days immediately before and after
period-end and trace each to underlying shipping documents, service
completion records, or system-of-record timestamps to confirm the
recognition date matches when the performance obligation was actually
satisfied, not when the invoice was generated or payment received.
Cutoff errors cluster right around period-end almost by definition, so
testing a window that straddles the cutoff date is far more
effective than sampling uniformly across the whole period.

revenue-recognition-testing#section-mult.title: Revenue Recognition Testing
revenue-recognition-testing#section-mult.heading: Multi-Element Arrangement Allocation
revenue-recognition-testing#section-mult.text:
## Multi-Element Arrangement Allocation

For contracts bundling multiple performance obligations (e.g. hardware,
implementation services, and a support subscription in one deal), test
that the total contract value was allocated across obligations based on
each element's standalone selling price, and that revenue for each
element was recognized only as that specific obligation was satisfied —
not all at contract signing. Look specifically for arrangements where a
disproportionate share of the total price was allocated to the element
recognized earliest, since that pattern can indicate revenue being
accelerated through allocation rather than genuine timing.

revenue-recognition-testing#section-cred.title: Revenue Recognition Testing
revenue-recognition-testing#section-cred.heading: Credit Memo and Reversal Review
revenue-recognition-testing#section-cred.text:
## Credit Memo and Reversal Review

Review credit memos and revenue reversals issued shortly after period-end
close, since a pattern of reversals concentrated right after close can
indicate revenue was recognized prematurely and then walked back once the
period was already reported. A credit memo tied to a genuine return or
service issue is normal; a cluster of reversals against large, late-
period transactions from the prior period warrants follow-up.

risk-assessment-methodology#summary.title: Audit Risk Assessment Methodology
risk-assessment-methodology#summary.text: Explains how inherent risk, control risk, and detection risk combine to set the nature, timing, and extent of testing for each audit area, and how the annual internal-audit plan is risk-ranked across the full auditable universe.

risk-assessment-methodology#section-the-.title: Audit Risk Assessment Methodology
risk-assessment-methodology#section-the-.heading: The Audit Risk Model
risk-assessment-methodology#section-the-.text:
## The Audit Risk Model

Audit risk is commonly decomposed into inherent risk (how susceptible an
area is to misstatement or failure before considering any controls),
control risk (how likely existing controls are to fail to prevent or
detect that misstatement), and detection risk (the risk that the audit's
own procedures fail to catch a misstatement that controls didn't). The
relationship between the three drives how much testing an area needs:
high inherent and control risk calls for lower acceptable detection risk,
which means more extensive testing.

risk-assessment-methodology#section-buil.title: Audit Risk Assessment Methodology
risk-assessment-methodology#section-buil.heading: Building the Auditable Universe Risk Ranking
risk-assessment-methodology#section-buil.text:
## Building the Auditable Universe Risk Ranking

The annual audit plan starts from a full inventory of auditable entities
(processes, systems, business units, entities) scored against consistent
risk factors — financial significance, complexity, regulatory exposure,
history of prior findings, time since last audit, and management's own
risk assessment input. Areas scoring highest get planned first and get
more hours; a low-risk area with no history of issues may go several
years between audits, while a high-risk area gets audited annually or
more often.

risk-assessment-methodology#section-refr.title: Audit Risk Assessment Methodology
risk-assessment-methodology#section-refr.heading: Refreshing the Assessment Mid-Cycle
risk-assessment-methodology#section-refr.text:
## Refreshing the Assessment Mid-Cycle

Risk rankings aren't static for the life of the annual plan — a
significant system change, a new regulatory requirement, a major
personnel turnover in a key process, or an emerging fraud pattern
elsewhere in the industry should trigger a re-ranking of the affected
area, potentially moving up a planned audit or adding an unplanned one.
Treat the annual risk assessment as the starting point for the plan, not
a fixed commitment that ignores what's actually happened since it was
built.

segregation-of-duties-review#summary.title: Segregation of Duties Review
segregation-of-duties-review#summary.text: Identifies whether any individual holds a combination of system access or process roles that would let them both commit and conceal an improper transaction without a second person's involvement.

segregation-of-duties-review#section-the.title: Segregation of Duties Review
segregation-of-duties-review#section-the.heading: The Core Risk
segregation-of-duties-review#section-the.text:
## The Core Risk

Segregation of duties (SoD) exists to make sure no single person can both
carry out and cover up a transaction end-to-end — e.g. creating a vendor
and approving payments to that vendor, or initiating a journal entry and
approving their own entry. The control isn't about distrust of any one
person; it's that a single point of control removes the natural check a
second reviewer provides, regardless of intent.

segregation-of-duties-review#section-bui.title: Segregation of Duties Review
segregation-of-duties-review#section-bui.heading: Building the SoD Conflict Matrix
segregation-of-duties-review#section-bui.text:
## Building the SoD Conflict Matrix

Start from a defined list of incompatible role combinations for the
relevant systems (e.g. "create vendor" + "approve payment," "post journal
entry" + "approve journal entry," "modify price master" + "approve sales
order override") agreed with process owners before testing begins. The
conflict matrix should be reviewed and updated periodically as system
roles change — testing against a stale matrix will miss real conflicts
introduced by new roles or missed by old ones.

segregation-of-duties-review#section-tes.title: Segregation of Duties Review
segregation-of-duties-review#section-tes.heading: Testing Actual System Access Against the Matrix
segregation-of-duties-review#section-tes.text:
## Testing Actual System Access Against the Matrix

Pull actual role/permission assignments from each in-scope system and run
them against the conflict matrix to identify every user holding an
incompatible combination — this should be a systematic comparison against
the full user population, not a sample, since SoD conflicts are
comparatively rare and a sample could easily miss the small number of
users who actually hold conflicting access. Each conflict identified needs
either a compensating control (e.g. a monitoring report someone
independent reviews) or a remediation plan to remove the conflicting
access.

segregation-of-duties-review#section-com.title: Segregation of Duties Review
segregation-of-duties-review#section-com.heading: Compensating Controls
segregation-of-duties-review#section-com.text:
## Compensating Controls

Where a genuine SoD conflict can't be eliminated (small teams are the most
common reason), confirm a compensating control actually operates — a
periodic report of transactions performed by the conflicted user,
reviewed and evidenced by someone independent of that user, at a
frequency tight enough to catch an issue before it compounds. A
compensating control that exists on paper but was never actually performed
during the period doesn't mitigate the conflict; test evidence of
performance, not just the existence of the control description.

sox-404-key-controls-walkthrough#summary.title: SOX 404 Key Controls Walkthrough
sox-404-key-controls-walkthrough#summary.text: A two-phase testing approach for SOX 404 key controls: Phase 1 walks through the control's design with the control owner to confirm it would prevent or detect a material misstatement if performed as described; Phase 2 samples actual instances of the control operating during the period to test whether it actually worked as designed.

sox-404-key-controls-walkthrough#section.title: SOX 404 Key Controls Walkthrough
sox-404-key-controls-walkthrough#section.heading: Objective
sox-404-key-controls-walkthrough#section.text:
## Objective

Confirm that a key control identified in the SOX 404 risk-and-controls
matrix (RCM) is both suitably designed and operating effectively, so
management and the external auditor can rely on it when concluding over
internal control over financial reporting (ICFR).

sox-404-key-controls-walkthrough#section.title: SOX 404 Key Controls Walkthrough
sox-404-key-controls-walkthrough#section.heading: Phase 1: Design Effectiveness
sox-404-key-controls-walkthrough#section.text:
## Phase 1: Design Effectiveness

Meet with the control owner and walk a single transaction end-to-end
through the control, from initiation to the point it's recorded. Confirm:
the control activity as performed matches the RCM's written description;
the control owner has the authority and system access needed to perform
it; and the control, if performed as described, would actually prevent or
detect a material misstatement — not just document that something
happened. Update the RCM narrative if the walkthrough surfaces a gap
between the documented control and the control as actually performed.

sox-404-key-controls-walkthrough#section.title: SOX 404 Key Controls Walkthrough
sox-404-key-controls-walkthrough#section.heading: Deficiency Classification
sox-404-key-controls-walkthrough#section.text:
## Deficiency Classification

Classify any exception found in either phase as a control deficiency,
significant deficiency, or material weakness based on the reasonable
possibility that a material misstatement would not be prevented or
detected. A single missed approval on a low-dollar, low-frequency control
is usually a deficiency; a broken control over a high-risk account with no
compensating control is a candidate for significant deficiency or worse.
Route the classification decision through the SOX PMO, not the individual
tester, since it affects the aggregate ICFR conclusion.

sox-404-key-controls-walkthrough#section.title: SOX 404 Key Controls Walkthrough
sox-404-key-controls-walkthrough#section.heading: Phase 2: Operating Effectiveness
sox-404-key-controls-walkthrough#section.text:
## Phase 2: Operating Effectiveness

Select a sample of instances where the control should have operated
during the testing period (see [Audit Sampling
Methodology](audit-sampling-methodology.md) for how sample size and
selection method are chosen) and test each instance for evidence the
control actually occurred — approval signatures, system timestamps,
exception reports reviewed and cleared. This step only starts once Phase
1 has confirmed the control is well-designed; testing operating
effectiveness on a control that isn't even properly designed wastes
effort on evidence that wouldn't matter anyway. A control that passes
Phase 1 but fails Phase 2 is a control that looks fine on paper but isn't
reliably performed; document it as an operating-effectiveness deficiency,
not a design deficiency.

vendor-master-data-control-testing#summa.title: Vendor Master Data Control Testing
vendor-master-data-control-testing#summa.text: Tests whether new-vendor and vendor-change requests in the ERP vendor master file go through required approval and duplicate-detection controls, since a weak vendor master file is a common enabler of fraudulent or duplicate payments.

vendor-master-data-control-testing#secti.title: Vendor Master Data Control Testing
vendor-master-data-control-testing#secti.heading: Why the Vendor Master File Matters
vendor-master-data-control-testing#secti.text:
## Why the Vendor Master File Matters

Every payment traces back to a vendor master record — bank account,
payment terms, tax ID. A vendor record created or changed without proper
review is one of the most common ways fictitious-vendor fraud and
duplicate payments get into the system, because once the master record
exists, downstream payments can look completely routine.

vendor-master-data-control-testing#secti.title: Vendor Master Data Control Testing
vendor-master-data-control-testing#secti.heading: New Vendor Setup Testing
vendor-master-data-control-testing#secti.text:
## New Vendor Setup Testing

Sample new vendor records created during the period and confirm each has:
a completed vendor onboarding form with a business justification, evidence
of a segregation-of-duties check (the requester cannot also be the
approver), and — for vendors above a dollar threshold — a W-9 or
equivalent tax form on file before the first payment. Flag any vendor
record where the bank account or address matches an existing employee
record; this is a specific, high-value fraud indicator, not just a
process gap.

vendor-master-data-control-testing#secti.title: Vendor Master Data Control Testing
vendor-master-data-control-testing#secti.heading: Vendor Change Testing
vendor-master-data-control-testing#secti.text:
## Vendor Change Testing

Changes to bank account or payment address on existing vendor records
carry similar risk to new-vendor setup, sometimes more — a change to a
long-standing, trusted vendor's bank details is a classic business email
compromise pattern. Sample vendor master change records and confirm each
bank-detail change has independent verification (e.g. a callback to a
phone number on file, not one provided in the change request itself)
before it took effect.

vendor-master-data-control-testing#secti.title: Vendor Master Data Control Testing
vendor-master-data-control-testing#secti.heading: Duplicate Vendor Detection
vendor-master-data-control-testing#secti.text:
## Duplicate Vendor Detection

Run the vendor master file through a fuzzy-matching check on name, tax
ID, address, and bank account to identify potential duplicate vendor
records — the same real-world vendor registered twice, deliberately or by
accident, which can enable duplicate payment or make spend harder to
analyze. Any match above the matching threshold should be investigated
and, where confirmed duplicate, merged or deactivated per the vendor
master governance procedure.
